warmup.text_pt: No C1, a gramática deixa de ser só "certo ou errado" e passa a ser uma questão de **atitude**. "I think" x "I'm thinking", "I wondered" x "I was wondering", "He's rude" x "He's being rude": cada escolha muda o que você comunica. Esta aula abre o nível com o tema **identidade**.

grammar.title: Verb forms: nuance and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Stative verbs no continuous** — verbos de estado (be, think, have, see, feel, love...) normalmente não vão para o continuous. Quando vão, o **sentido muda**:
- **be** → comportamento temporário: "He **is** rude." (é grosso) x "He**'s being** rude." (está sendo grosso agora)
- **think** → opinião x processo: "I **think** it's a good idea." x "I**'m thinking** about moving abroad." (considerando)
- **see** → ver x encontrar/namorar: "I **see** what you mean." x "I**'m seeing** the doctor at 3." / "She**'s seeing** someone."
- **have** → posse x atividade: "I **have** two sisters." x "We**'re having** dinner."
- **love / like** no continuous → entusiasmo informal com algo atual: "I**'m loving** this new job!"

**2. Passado e continuous para distanciamento ("tentative")** — tornam pedidos e opiniões mais suaves e educados:
- "I **was wondering** if you could..." (mais educado que "I wonder")
- "I **was hoping** we could talk." / "We **were thinking** of leaving early."
- "**Did** you **want** a coffee?" (oferta educada, sobre o presente)
- "I **thought** you might like this."

**3. Always / constantly / forever + continuous** → hábito irritante ou marcante:
- "He's **always interrupting** me!" / "She was **forever** losing her keys."
- Também pode ser positivo: "She's **always doing** nice things for people."

**4. Present perfect para novidades** (notícias, anúncios), seguido do past simple para os detalhes:
- "Scientists **have discovered** a new species. It **was found** in the Amazon last month."

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, usamos o **futuro do pretérito** para suavizar ("Eu **gostaria** de saber..."). Em inglês, o mesmo efeito vem do **passado continuous**: "I **was wondering**..." — é uma das marcas mais claras de um falante C1.

dialogue.title: You're being very quiet
dialogue.context_pt: Dois amigos conversam num café; um deles está pensando em mudar de vida.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.en: You're being very quiet today. Is everything OK?
lines.pt: Você está muito quieto hoje. Está tudo bem?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: Yeah, sorry. I've just got a lot on my mind. I'm thinking of leaving the bank.
lines.pt: Sim, desculpa. Só estou com muita coisa na cabeça. Estou pensando em sair do banco.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.en: Really? You've been there for, what, eight years? That's so out of character for you.
lines.pt: Sério? Você está lá há, sei lá, oito anos? Isso não tem nada a ver com você.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: I know. But deep down, I've never really felt like a banker. I'm always telling people what I do and then changing the subject.
lines.pt: Eu sei. Mas, no fundo, nunca me senti realmente um bancário. Vivo dizendo às pessoas o que faço e mudando de assunto.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.en: So what would you do instead?
lines.pt: E o que você faria no lugar?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: I've been taking photography courses at weekends, and honestly, I'm loving it. I was wondering if you'd look at my portfolio, actually.
lines.pt: Tenho feito cursos de fotografia nos fins de semana e, sinceramente, estou amando. Na verdade, eu queria saber se você daria uma olhada no meu portfólio.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.en: Of course! I'd love to. I think it takes courage to reinvent yourself at thirty-five.
lines.pt: Claro! Adoraria. Acho que é preciso coragem para se reinventar aos trinta e cinco.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: Or madness. My parents certainly think so. But I'd rather be true to myself than spend another eight years pretending.
lines.pt: Ou loucura. Meus pais com certeza acham que é. Mas prefiro ser fiel a mim mesmo do que passar mais oito anos fingindo.

listening.title: The stories we tell about ourselves
listening.context_pt: Trecho de um podcast de psicologia sobre identidade narrativa.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Psychologists who study what they call "narrative identity" argue that we don't just have experiences — we turn them into stories, and those stories become who we are. The researcher Dan McAdams has spent decades studying these life stories. One pattern that comes up again and again is what he calls a "redemption sequence": a story in which something bad turns into something good. "I lost my job, but it led me to find my real calling." Research in this area suggests that people who tell their lives this way tend to report higher well-being. Now, I'm not saying we should invent happy endings. But it's worth asking: what story are you telling about yourself? And is it the only possible version? Because, as it turns out, we have more freedom to rewrite it than we usually think.

questions.q: What is "narrative identity"?
questions.answer: The idea that we turn our experiences into stories, which become who we are.

questions.q: What is a "redemption sequence"?
questions.answer: A story in which something bad turns into something good.

questions.q: What does research suggest about people who tell their lives this way?
questions.answer: They tend to report higher well-being.

questions.q: What is the speaker's final point?
questions.answer: We have more freedom to rewrite our story than we think.

reading.title: The myth of the fixed self
reading.text: Ask people whether their personality will change much over the next ten years and most will say no. Ask them how much it has changed over the past ten years, however, and they will readily admit that it has changed considerably. Psychologists Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson called this the "end of history illusion": at every age, we seem to believe that the person we are today is, more or less, the finished product. Their study, published in Science in 2013, surveyed thousands of adults and found that people consistently underestimated how much their values, preferences and personalities would change in the future. The illusion has practical consequences. Because we assume our current tastes will last, we may pay too much today for things our future selves won't value — a tattoo, say, or a ticket to see a favourite band a decade from now. Longitudinal research on personality offers a more nuanced picture still. Traits such as conscientiousness and emotional stability tend to increase gradually throughout adulthood, a pattern sometimes described as "maturation". None of this means that we are endlessly changeable; there is real continuity in who we are. But it does suggest that the question "Who am I?" is better answered in pencil than in ink. The self, it seems, is less a statue than a river.

questions.q: What is the "end of history illusion"?
questions.answer: The belief, at every age, that our current self is more or less the finished product.

questions.q: What did the 2013 study find?
questions.answer: People consistently underestimated how much they would change in the future.

questions.q: What practical consequence of the illusion is mentioned?
questions.answer: We may pay too much now for things our future selves won't value.

questions.q: What does the metaphor "less a statue than a river" mean?
questions.answer: The self keeps changing and flowing rather than being fixed.

writing.model:
The person I used to think I was

For most of my twenties, I was convinced I was an introvert. I was always making excuses to leave parties early, and I genuinely believed that I simply wasn't "a people person". It was a label I had picked up at school, where a teacher once described me as "quiet but reliable", and I wore it for years without questioning it.

Things started to shift when I moved to Recife for work. I didn't know anyone, so I had no choice but to start conversations — with neighbours, with colleagues, with the man who sold coconut water on the corner. To my surprise, I was enjoying it. I remember calling my sister after a few months and saying, "I think I'm being someone else here." She laughed and replied that perhaps I was finally being myself.

Looking back, I suspect I wasn't really an introvert at all. I was anxious, which is a very different thing. Being quiet had felt safer than risking rejection, and the label gave me a convenient explanation.

None of this means I've become the life and soul of the party. I still need time alone to recharge, and there are evenings when I'd much rather read than go out. But I've stopped thinking of myself as a fixed type. These days, if someone asks me whether I'm an introvert or an extrovert, I usually answer, "It depends on the day."

If I could talk to my younger self, I think I'd simply say: "I was wondering whether you'd ever considered that the story you tell about yourself might be wrong." Labels can be useful, but they are descriptions, not destinies.

culture_note.title: "Where are you from?"
culture_note.text_pt: Em países multiculturais como Reino Unido, EUA e Canadá, a pergunta **"Where are you from?"** pode soar delicada quando insistida ("But where are you *really* from?"), pois sugere que a pessoa não pertence ao lugar. Alternativas mais abertas: **"Where did you grow up?"** ou **"Where's home for you?"**.

grammar.title: Ellipsis and substitution
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Substituição** = trocar uma parte da frase por uma palavra curta. **Elipse** = simplesmente omitir o que já está claro.

**1. so / not** substituem uma oração inteira depois de think, hope, expect, suppose, believe, guess, be afraid, appear, seem:
- "Is she coming?" — "I **think so**." / "I **hope not**." / "I'm **afraid not**."
- Negativa com think/believe/expect: **I don't think so** (mais natural que "I think not", que soa formal).
- **If so / If not**: "Are you free on Friday? **If so**, let's meet."
- Formal: **do so** substitui verbo + complemento: "Applicants must register online. Those who fail to **do so** will be excluded."

**2. one / ones** substituem substantivos contáveis:
- "I don't like this shirt. Can I see the red **one**?" / "These shoes are nicer than the old **ones**."
- ⚠️ Não use one com incontáveis: ❌ "I prefer the French one wine" → "I prefer French wine."

**3. Infinitivo reduzido (to)** — repete-se só o **to**:
- "Do you want to come?" — "I'd **love to**." / "I don't **want to**." / "I **meant to**, but I forgot."

**4. Auxiliares (elipse do verbo principal):**
- "I can't speak Japanese, but my sister **can**."
- "She said she'd call, and she **did**."
- "I haven't finished yet, but I **will have** by Friday."

**5. Elipse em orações coordenadas** (muito comum na escrita):
- "Some of the participants spoke English, others (spoke) Spanish."
- "I'd like to help, but (I) can't."

listening.title: Does language shape thought?
listening.context_pt: Uma linguista explica, numa aula aberta, pesquisas sobre língua e pensamento.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Does the language you speak change the way you think? For much of the twentieth century, the strong version of this idea — that language determines thought — was largely rejected. But a weaker version has gained support. The cognitive scientist Lera Boroditsky and others have studied, for instance, an Aboriginal community in Australia, the Kuuk Thaayorre, whose language uses cardinal directions — north, south, east, west — instead of "left" and "right". Speakers have been reported to stay remarkably well oriented, even indoors. Other studies have looked at colour: Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and some experiments found that Russian speakers were slightly faster at distinguishing those shades. Does this mean we're prisoners of our language? Most researchers would say not. But it does suggest that each language trains our attention in particular ways — and that learning another one can show us the world from a slightly different angle.

questions.q: Which version of the idea was largely rejected?
questions.answer: The strong version: that language determines thought.

questions.q: What is special about Kuuk Thaayorre?
questions.answer: It uses cardinal directions instead of left and right.

questions.q: What did some experiments find about Russian speakers?
questions.answer: They were slightly faster at distinguishing light and dark blue.

questions.q: What is the speaker's conclusion?
questions.answer: Languages train our attention in particular ways; learning one shows a new angle.

reading.title: The translator's dilemma
reading.text: Every translator faces the same impossible choice: be faithful to the words or to the meaning. Translate too literally, and the result may be accurate but lifeless; translate too freely, and you risk replacing the author's voice with your own. Nowhere is this clearer than with humour, poetry and culturally loaded words. Take the Portuguese "jeitinho". A dictionary might offer "knack" or "way around something", but neither conveys the mixture of creativity, flexibility and occasional rule-bending the word suggests to Brazilians. A translator can choose to keep the original word and explain it, to find an approximate equivalent, or to rewrite the sentence entirely. Each option gains something and loses something. Machine translation has transformed the field in recent years. For everyday texts — instructions, emails, the gist of a news article — modern tools are remarkably good, and many professional translators now use them as a first draft. Literary translation, however, remains a stubbornly human craft. A novel's rhythm, ambiguity and wordplay depend on choices that require an understanding not only of two languages but of two cultures. Perhaps the best definition of a good translation is one that makes the reader forget it is one. If so, the translator's greatest achievement is to become invisible — which may explain why so few readers can name the translators of their favourite books.

questions.q: What is the translator's "impossible choice"?
questions.answer: To be faithful to the words or to the meaning.

questions.q: Why is "jeitinho" hard to translate?
questions.answer: No English word conveys its mix of creativity, flexibility and rule-bending.

questions.q: How do many professionals use machine translation?
questions.answer: As a first draft.

questions.q: Why does literary translation remain human?
questions.answer: Rhythm, ambiguity and wordplay require understanding two languages and two cultures.

writing.model:
Five Brazilian words the world needs

Every language has words that others envy. English speakers have borrowed "schadenfreude" from German and "hygge" from Danish; perhaps it's time they borrowed a few from Brazilian Portuguese too.

1. Saudade. Often described as untranslatable, saudade is a bittersweet longing for someone or something absent. Is it the same as nostalgia? Not quite. You can feel it for a person who is alive and well, or even for a future that hasn't happened yet.

2. Cafuné. The act of gently running your fingers through someone's hair. Many languages have no single word for it; Portuguese does, which may say something about how much Brazilians value physical affection.

3. Gambiarra. An improvised, often ingenious fix — holding a broken door shut with a chair, say. Engineers might frown at it; most Brazilians, if they're honest, admire it.

4. Jeitinho. Closely related to gambiarra but applied to rules rather than objects, jeitinho means finding a creative way around an obstacle. Is it always positive? I don't think so. It can describe both admirable flexibility and questionable shortcuts.

5. Xodó. Someone's xodó is their favourite person or thing — the one they spoil and adore. A grandmother might call her youngest grandchild her xodó; a teenager might use the word for a new phone.

What do these words reveal? Perhaps a culture that values warmth, improvisation and emotional honesty. Of course, no list can capture a whole country, and this one doesn't try to. But if English speakers ever need a word for the feeling of missing a place they've never been to, they'll know where to find one.

grammar.title: Emphatic structures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. do / does / did enfático** (em frases afirmativas) — reforça, contrasta ou corrige:
- "I **do** like your new haircut!" (gosto mesmo)
- "You never listen to me!" — "I **do** listen!" (contradizer)
- "She **did** warn us, to be fair." (admitir)
- No imperativo, soa insistente e caloroso: "**Do** come in!" / "**Do** sit down."
- Na fala, o **do** é sempre **acentuado**.

**2. Fronting** — mover um elemento para o início para dar destaque:
- **Adjetivo/advérbio + as + sujeito + verbo** (concessão = "por mais... que"):
  "**Strange as it may seem**, ..." / "**Tired as she was**, she kept going." / "**Hard as I tried**, I couldn't settle in."
- **Much as** + oração (= although, "por mais que"): "**Much as I love** my hometown, I couldn't live there again."
- Objeto no início (estilo literário/falado): "**That** I don't understand." / "**Some things** you never forget."

**3. so / such... that**
- **so + adjetivo/advérbio + that**: "The city was **so** noisy **that** I couldn't sleep."
- **such + (a/an) + adjetivo + substantivo + that**: "It was **such a** warm welcome **that** I cried."
- **so much / many / little / few + substantivo**: "There were **so many** people **that**..."

**4. Inversão com so / such** (formal/literário):
- "**So** strong **was** the feeling **that** I cried."
- "**Such was** her homesickness **that** she flew back after a month."

rows: Small as it is, our flat feels like home.
Much as I love her, she drives me mad.

grammar.tip_pt: **"Por mais que..."** em inglês tem várias formas elegantes: **Much as** I love it..., **However much** I love it..., **Hard as** I tried... Usar uma delas numa redação ou na prova oral é uma marca clara de C1.

listening.title: Third culture kids
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre crianças que crescem entre culturas.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: The term "third culture kids" was coined in the 1950s by the American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem, who studied children of families living abroad. The idea is that these children grow up between their parents' culture and the culture of the country where they live, and end up creating a third culture of their own. Ask one of them "Where are you from?" and you may get a long pause. Many describe a feeling of belonging everywhere and nowhere. Strange as it may seem, they often feel most at home with other third culture kids, regardless of nationality. There are clear advantages: adaptability, language skills, an ability to see situations from several perspectives. But there are challenges too. Repeated goodbyes can make some people reluctant to form deep attachments. So common is this experience that many international schools now run programmes to help students deal with transitions.

questions.q: Who coined the term, and when?
questions.answer: Ruth Hill Useem, an American sociologist, in the 1950s.

questions.q: What is the "third culture"?
questions.answer: A culture of their own, created between their parents' culture and the host culture.

questions.q: Who do they often feel most at home with?
questions.answer: Other third culture kids.

questions.q: What challenge is mentioned?
questions.answer: Repeated goodbyes can make them reluctant to form deep attachments.

reading.title: What makes a place home?
reading.text: Much as we talk about home as a place, researchers who study belonging suggest it is better understood as a set of relationships. In one influential framework, environmental psychologists describe "place attachment" as developing through three overlapping dimensions: the people we share a place with, the meaningful experiences we have there, and the physical features we come to know intimately — the smell of a particular bakery, the sound of the street at dawn. This helps explain a phenomenon that puzzles many migrants. Returning to their hometown after years away, they find the streets unchanged but the feeling gone. Their friends have moved on, the rhythms of daily life have changed, and they themselves are no longer the same people. Home, it turns out, does not stay where we left it. Brazil offers a vivid illustration. Over the twentieth century, millions of people moved from the countryside and the Northeast to cities in the Southeast. Many of them recreated home in their new neighbourhoods through food, music and festivals: the forró halls and Northeastern fairs of São Paulo are a direct result of this. Such was the scale of the movement that it transformed the culture of the cities that received it. Perhaps the lesson is that belonging is not something we find but something we build. Small as they are, the daily rituals of a place — a greeting from a neighbour, a familiar route to work — slowly turn a city into home.

questions.q: How do researchers suggest home is better understood?
questions.answer: As a set of relationships rather than just a place.

questions.q: What are the three dimensions of place attachment?
questions.answer: People, meaningful experiences and physical features.

questions.q: Why do returning migrants feel the place has changed?
questions.answer: Their friends have moved on, routines have changed, and they themselves have changed.

questions.q: How did internal migrants recreate home in São Paulo?
questions.answer: Through food, music and festivals (forró halls, Northeastern fairs).

writing.model:
The place I call home

When people ask me where I'm from, I usually say Campina Grande, because that's where I was born. But if they asked where home is, I'd have to think much harder.

I left Paraíba at eighteen to study in Porto Alegre, more than three thousand kilometres away. The first winter was so cold that I slept in two jumpers and a hat. Such was the shock — the climate, the accent, the reserved way people greeted each other — that I seriously considered going back after the first semester.

I didn't, of course. Slowly, the city began to change, or perhaps I did. I found a bakery where the owner remembered my order. I joined a football team made up almost entirely of other "outsiders" from different states. I learned to drink chimarrão, and, strange as it may seem, I came to love it.

That was fifteen years ago. Today, I have a flat, a partner, a dog and a job I enjoy. I've put down roots. And yet, every June, I do feel a pull towards the Northeast. Much as I love Porto Alegre, nothing compares to the festa junina in Campina Grande: the forró, the bonfires, the smell of canjica and pamonha.

So where is home? I've come to believe that it isn't a single place. Home is wherever my people are, and wherever I feel I can be fully myself. Some days that's a street in the South; other days, it's a memory of the Northeast.

I do sometimes envy people who have never left the place where they were born. But I wouldn't change my two homes for anything.

culture_note.title: Migração interna no Brasil

Essa migração moldou a cultura dessas cidades — do forró à culinária — e também gerou preconceitos que ainda existem. Em inglês, o fenômeno é descrito como **internal migration** ou **rural-to-urban migration**.

grammar.title: Spoken discourse markers and vague language
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Discourse markers da fala** — organizam a conversa e mostram sua atitude:
- **Mudar / voltar ao assunto:** anyway, by the way, incidentally, speaking of which, as I was saying
- **Acrescentar uma ressalva:** **mind you** ("se bem que"), **that said / having said that**, then again
- **Coincidência / informação relevante:** **as it happens**, actually, funnily enough
- **Reconsiderar:** **come to think of it**, now that I think about it, on second thoughts
- **Resumir / concluir:** so, basically, at the end of the day, all in all
- **Ganhar tempo / suavizar:** well, I mean, you know, let me see

"The hotel was a bit far from the centre. **Mind you**, the view was incredible."
"Are you going to the conference? — **As it happens**, I'm giving a talk there."

**2. Vague language** — imprecisão **intencional**, típica da fala natural (não é erro!):
- **Aproximar números/horários:** about, around, roughly, **or so**, **-ish** (sevenish, fortyish), give or take
- **Categorias:** **and stuff (like that)**, **and things**, **or something (like that)**, **and so on**
- **Suavizar:** **sort of / kind of**, a bit, slightly, quite
- **Palavras "coringa":** thing, stuff, whatsit, thingy (muito informal)

"I've been there twenty times **or so**." / "She's **sort of** shy at first." / "We talked about work **and stuff**."

⚠️ **Registro:** vague language é para a **fala informal**. Em redações e e-mails formais, seja preciso.

grammar.tip_pt: O equivalente ao nosso "**tipo**" é **like** ("It was, like, really weird") — muito comum entre jovens, mas excessivo soa imaturo. **Sort of / kind of** são mais neutros.

listening.title: In defence of small talk
listening.context_pt: Um comentarista de rádio defende a importância do small talk.

lines.speaker: Commentator
lines.en: Small talk has a pretty bad reputation. People call it shallow, fake, a waste of time. But, as it happens, research suggests otherwise. In one well-known study, the psychologists Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn asked people to have a brief, friendly exchange with a barista instead of just ordering and leaving. Those who chatted reported a better mood and a greater sense of belonging. Sandstrom has also found that our interactions with so-called "weak ties" — the neighbour, the bus driver, the person at the gym — contribute to our happiness more than we tend to assume. Mind you, I'm not saying you should corner strangers and talk about the weather for half an hour. But a two-minute chat is sort of like social glue. It's how relationships start. Come to think of it, most of my close friends began as people I made small talk with.

questions.q: What reputation does small talk have?
questions.answer: Shallow, fake, a waste of time.

questions.q: What happened to people who chatted with the barista?

reading.title: The strength of weak ties
reading.text: In 1973, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a deliberately paradoxical title: "The Strength of Weak Ties". Studying how people in a Boston suburb had found their jobs, he noticed something surprising. Many had heard about the opportunity not from close friends but from acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally. His explanation was elegant. Our close friends tend to move in the same circles we do, so they mostly know what we already know. Acquaintances, by contrast, connect us to different networks and therefore to new information. The idea has since become one of the most cited in the social sciences, and recent research has largely supported it. A large study of LinkedIn users, published in Science in 2022, found that moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility. That said, weak ties do more than help us find work. They also seem to matter for our well-being. A quick chat with a neighbour or a familiar face at the market can make a city feel friendlier and less anonymous. Perhaps this is why so many people felt strangely lonely during the pandemic lockdowns, even when they kept in touch with close friends online: what had disappeared were the small, casual encounters that once filled their days. Small talk, it seems, is not so small after all.

questions.q: What did Granovetter notice about how people found jobs?
questions.answer: Many heard about opportunities from acquaintances, not close friends.

questions.q: Why are weak ties useful, according to his explanation?
questions.answer: They connect us to different networks and new information.

questions.q: What did the 2022 LinkedIn study find?
questions.answer: Moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility.

questions.q: Why might people have felt lonely during lockdowns?
questions.answer: The small, casual encounters with weak ties had disappeared.

writing.task: Write an informal blog post (250–300 words) titled "How I learned to love small talk". Write in a natural, conversational style using at least six discourse markers and four examples of vague language.
writing.task_pt: Escreva um post informal de blog (250–300 palavras) intitulado "Como aprendi a amar o small talk". Use um estilo natural e conversacional, com pelo menos seis discourse markers e quatro exemplos de vague language.
writing.model:
How I learned to love small talk

I'll be honest: for most of my life, I hated small talk. Chatting about the weather, the traffic, the weekend — it all seemed sort of pointless. If I wanted to talk to someone, I wanted to talk about something real.

That changed about three years ago, when I started working from home. At first, I loved it. No commute, no office politics, no awkward conversations by the coffee machine. Then, after six months or so, I noticed something strange. I felt lonely — and not because I missed my close friends. I spoke to them all the time. What I missed were the tiny, meaningless chats: the security guard asking about my weekend, the colleague who always complained about the air conditioning, that kind of thing.

As it happens, I'd just read an article about "weak ties" — the acquaintances who make up a big part of our social world. Apparently, brief exchanges with them can genuinely improve our mood. So I tried an experiment. For a month, I made a point of chatting to at least one stranger a day: the woman at the bakery, the guy who walks the same dog route as me, people at the gym and so on.

The results? Well, I didn't make any best friends. Mind you, I did start looking forward to my morning bread run. Come to think of it, I also ended up joining a running group thanks to the dog guy.

Anyway, the point is this: small talk isn't really about the weather. It's about saying, "I see you, and I'm friendly." That said, I still draw the line at talking about the traffic for more than two minutes!

culture_note.title: Small talk pelo mundo
culture_note.text_pt: Nos EUA, small talk com desconhecidos (no elevador, na fila) é comum e esperado. No Reino Unido, o **tempo** é o tema clássico — e reclamar dele é quase um ritual. Na Finlândia, ao contrário, o silêncio entre desconhecidos é confortável e normal. Brasileiros costumam ser calorosos e pessoais rapidamente — às vezes **pessoais demais** para padrões anglo-saxões (idade, salário, religião e vida amorosa são temas a evitar no início).

Vague: -ish, or so, and stuff, sort of / kind of.
Vague language = fala informal; em textos formais, seja preciso.
